title: Unit conversions in analytical models
description: A practical modeling pattern for preserving captured units, conversion provenance, and normalized values without hiding numeric assumptions.
lead: Analytical models often need one number for aggregation and another record of what actually happened. Unit conversion is where that tension becomes visible: a dashboard wants total quantity in a standard unit, while a data engineer needs to preserve whether the source system captured cases, eaches, kilograms, pounds, pallets, or some product-specific package size. The safest pattern is not to overwrite the captured value. Store the original unit and quantity, store the normalized value used for analysis, and store the conversion rule that produced it.

sections.heading: The problem with one quantity column
paragraphs: A single quantity column looks simple until two rows use different units. Suppose a hypothetical retail shipment model receives three lines for the same product: 3 cases shipped on January 5, 8 eaches shipped on January 6, and 2 cases shipped on February 2. If a report sums the raw quantity column, it returns 13. That number is not a physical quantity. It is the sum of 3 cases, 8 eaches, and 2 cases after the unit label was discarded.

The opposite mistake is also common: convert everything to a base unit and keep only the converted value. That makes aggregation easier, but it removes the evidence needed to explain the number. If a store disputes a shipment, the operational record probably says 3 cases, not 36 eaches. If the package definition changes from 12 eaches per case to 10 eaches per case, a later analyst needs to know which conversion rule was used for each historical row.

Kimball’s dimensional modeling guidance treats multiple units of measure as an explicit modeling concern rather than a formatting problem. The practical conclusion for analytical models is straightforward: original values and converted values serve different purposes, so they should be different fields.

sections.heading: Calculation rules for normalized values
paragraphs: A unit-safe fact table should make the conversion path visible. At minimum, a transaction-level fact should carry the captured quantity, the captured unit, the normalized quantity, the normalized unit, and a conversion identifier. The conversion identifier should point to a rule that includes the factor, product or unit family where applicable, effective dates, and rounding behavior.

Use a base unit that is additive for the analysis you expect. For a sellable item, that might be each. For liquid volume, it might be milliliters or liters. For weight, it might be grams or kilograms. Do not treat all units as interchangeable just because they are numbers. A count of eaches is not naturally convertible to kilograms unless a product-specific net weight assumption is part of the rule.

A durable calculation rule looks like this: normalized_quantity = captured_quantity × conversion_numerator ÷ conversion_denominator. Storing the factor as numerator and denominator avoids some ambiguity around repeating decimals. For example, pounds to ounces is 16 over 1, while ounces to pounds is 1 over 16. Decimal arithmetic is usually preferable for analytical storage; binary floating point can introduce representation artifacts that are distracting or material depending on precision and downstream rounding.

Rounding should be a named rule, not an accidental side effect. For aggregation, the usual analytical preference is to store enough precision in the normalized value and round only for presentation. If the business requires line-level rounding, preserve that rule in the conversion metadata because totals can differ when rounding happens before aggregation instead of after aggregation.
bullets: Store captured_quantity and captured_unit_key exactly as received from the source, except for clearly documented source cleansing.
Store normalized_quantity and normalized_unit_key for additive reporting.
Store conversion_rule_key or conversion_version_key so the conversion can be explained later.
Store effective dates on conversion rules when package sizes or unit definitions can change over time.
Reject or quarantine rows where no valid conversion rule exists for the transaction date and product context.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: The following example is hypothetical. It models one product whose case pack changes over time. Before February 1, one case contains 12 eaches. Starting February 1, one case contains 10 eaches. The source events must remain visible because the operational shipment line was captured in cases or eaches, not only in normalized eaches.

The correct normalized total is 64 eaches: 3 January cases × 12 = 36, plus 8 eaches × 1 = 8, plus 2 February cases × 10 = 20. Revenue is 152, so revenue per normalized each is 152 ÷ 64 = 2.375. If someone divides revenue by the raw summed quantity, they get 152 ÷ 13 = about 11.692 per mixed unit, which has no stable meaning. If someone applies only the current case pack of 10 to all rows, the total becomes 58 eaches. If someone applies only the older pack of 12 to all rows, the total becomes 68 eaches. Both are explainable errors caused by losing conversion provenance or effective dating.
This SQL is illustrative. It is meant to show the modeling shape and arithmetic, not to claim execution in a particular warehouse engine.

codeExamples.code:
with fact_shipment_line as (
    select 1 as shipment_line_id, date '2026-01-05' as shipped_at, 'SKU-TEA' as sku, 3.0000 as captured_quantity, 'CASE' as captured_unit, 72.00 as revenue
    union all select 2, date '2026-01-06', 'SKU-TEA', 8.0000, 'EACH', 20.00
    union all select 3, date '2026-02-02', 'SKU-TEA', 2.0000, 'CASE', 60.00
),
dim_unit_conversion as (
    select 'SKU-TEA_CASE_EACH_2026_01' as conversion_rule_key, 'SKU-TEA' as sku, 'CASE' as from_unit, 'EACH' as to_unit,
           12.0000 as conversion_numerator, 1.0000 as conversion_denominator,
           date '2026-01-01' as effective_from, date '2026-02-01' as effective_to_exclusive
    union all select 'SKU-TEA_CASE_EACH_2026_02', 'SKU-TEA', 'CASE', 'EACH', 10.0000, 1.0000, date '2026-02-01', null
    union all select 'SKU-TEA_EACH_EACH_ALWAYS', 'SKU-TEA', 'EACH', 'EACH', 1.0000, 1.0000, date '1900-01-01', null
),
converted as (
    select
        f.shipment_line_id,
        f.shipped_at,
        f.sku,
        f.captured_quantity,
        f.captured_unit,
        c.to_unit as normalized_unit,
        f.captured_quantity * c.conversion_numerator / c.conversion_denominator as normalized_quantity,
        c.conversion_rule_key,
        f.revenue
    from fact_shipment_line f
    join dim_unit_conversion c
      on f.sku = c.sku
     and f.captured_unit = c.from_unit
     and c.to_unit = 'EACH'
     and f.shipped_at >= c.effective_from
     and (c.effective_to_exclusive is null or f.shipped_at < c.effective_to_exclusive)
)
select
    sku,
    sum(captured_quantity) as raw_quantity_sum_do_not_use_for_units,
    sum(normalized_quantity) as normalized_each_quantity,
    sum(revenue) as revenue,
    sum(revenue) / nullif(sum(normalized_quantity), 0) as revenue_per_each
from converted
group by sku;

sections.heading: A modeling pattern that keeps both truth and utility
paragraphs: A useful pattern is to separate the event, the conversion rule, and the derived analytical value. The event says what the source captured. The conversion rule says how to translate the captured unit into the analytical base unit. The fact table can store the derived value for performance and simplicity, but that value should be reproducible from the captured value and the rule key.

This is similar in spirit to a Type 0 attribute: some fields should retain the original value rather than being restated when definitions change. The captured unit on a shipment line is such a field. If the source event said CASE, the analytical model should not mutate that field to EACH merely because the warehouse uses each as its additive base unit.

The conversion dimension should be scoped carefully. Some conversions are global within a unit family, such as 1 kilogram = 1000 grams. Others are product-specific, such as 1 case of SKU-TEA = 12 eaches in January and 10 eaches in February. Others are not valid without additional assumptions. For example, converting a bag count to kilograms requires a product weight assumption; converting a volume to a mass requires a density assumption. Those assumptions belong in the conversion provenance, not in undocumented transformation code.
bullets: Fact fields: captured_quantity, captured_unit_key, normalized_quantity, normalized_unit_key, conversion_rule_key.
Conversion fields: from_unit_key, to_unit_key, numerator, denominator, product_key when needed, effective_from, effective_to, rounding_rule, rule_source.
Quality fields: conversion_status, conversion_error_reason, and possibly normalized_quantity_is_estimated when estimates are allowed.
Audit fields: source_system, source_event_id, loaded_at, and transformation_version where your platform uses one.

sections.heading: Counterexamples that catch bad models
paragraphs: The fastest way to find a weak unit model is to construct a small example where the wrong answer looks plausible. Mixed units are especially dangerous because bad totals often remain within a believable range.

Counterexample one: raw quantity summation. The hypothetical shipment lines sum to 13 raw units. A dashboard might show 13 shipped units without erroring. The number is wrong because the model has added cases and eaches. A useful semantic layer should make this hard or impossible by exposing normalized_quantity for additive measures and treating captured_quantity as descriptive unless grouped by captured unit.

Counterexample two: current conversion restatement. If the model joins all historical case rows to the current case definition of 10 eaches, January’s 3 cases become 30 eaches instead of 36. The report is internally consistent but historically wrong. The diagnostic is to ask whether a previously published historical total can change solely because a packaging definition changed. If yes, the model is probably using a Type 1-style overwrite where it needs dated conversion provenance.

Counterexample three: incompatible dimensions. Suppose a customer order contains 2 cases of tea bags and 4 kilograms of loose tea. Both are tea quantities, but they are not additive under a single unit unless the model has a rule for converting the cases into weight or the kilograms into sellable units. Without that rule, a total tea quantity is a label, not a measurement.

sections.heading: Diagnostic queries and tests
paragraphs: Unit conversion should have tests at the same level as primary keys and not-null checks because a missing conversion can silently change an aggregate. The goal is not to prove that every business assumption is perfect. The goal is to prevent untraceable arithmetic.

A first test finds transaction rows with no conversion rule. In most analytical models, those rows should be rejected from the normalized aggregate or surfaced with a conversion_status that prevents accidental inclusion. A second test finds measures where the same aggregate mixes captured units. That is not always an error, but it is a prompt to verify that the report uses normalized quantities. A third test checks that each fact row matches only one conversion rule for its product, unit, target unit, and transaction date. Overlapping effective dates create duplicate joins and inflated totals.

For the hypothetical example above, the expected aggregate is 64 normalized eaches and 152 revenue. Keeping that expected result in a small fixture is valuable because it exercises the two failure modes that matter: mixed units and time-varying conversion rules.

codeExamples.code:
-- Rows that cannot be converted to the model's additive base unit.
select
    f.shipment_line_id,
    f.sku,
    f.shipped_at,
    f.captured_quantity,
    f.captured_unit
from fact_shipment_line f
left join dim_unit_conversion c
  on f.sku = c.sku
 and f.captured_unit = c.from_unit
 and c.to_unit = 'EACH'
 and f.shipped_at >= c.effective_from
 and (c.effective_to_exclusive is null or f.shipped_at < c.effective_to_exclusive)
where c.conversion_rule_key is null;

-- Groups where captured quantities should not be summed without unit context.
select
    sku,
    count(distinct captured_unit) as captured_unit_count
from fact_shipment_line
group by sku
having count(distinct captured_unit) > 1;

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and practical boundaries
paragraphs: Storing both original and normalized values costs more columns and more modeling discipline. That cost is usually smaller than the cost of explaining why a shipment, consumption, or inventory trend changed after a unit definition was updated. The important tradeoff is deciding which values are authoritative. Captured fields are authoritative for what the source said. Normalized fields are authoritative for additive analytics under a named conversion rule. Neither field replaces the other.

Avoid making conversion provenance too vague. A column named conversion_factor is better than nothing, but it is not enough when factors vary by product, date, source, or rounding policy. A conversion_rule_key gives downstream users a join path to the assumptions behind the number.

Also avoid pushing every possible unit into one universal dimension without context. Global unit definitions are useful, but business packaging is often contextual. A case, pack, bundle, or pallet may mean different quantities for different products or at different times. The model should represent that context explicitly.

This article does not cover tax treatment, accounting recognition, or currency conversion date policy. Those topics have separate rules. The unit-conversion problem here is narrower: preserve the original measurement, compute an additive normalized measurement, and keep enough provenance to reproduce the calculation.

takeaways: Do not overwrite captured units with normalized units. Preserve the original quantity and unit beside the converted value.
Normalized quantities are only trustworthy when they point to a specific conversion rule, including product context and effective dates when those matter.
Raw quantities are descriptive unless they share the same unit. Aggregates should use normalized quantities with compatible base units.
Small counterexample fixtures are enough to catch common failures: summing mixed units, applying current conversions to history, and converting between incompatible dimensions.

title: Exchange-rate direction and inversion
description: A practical guide to modeling exchange-rate direction so currency normalization uses multiplication and division correctly.
lead: Currency normalization often fails for a simple reason: the rate is correct, the amount is correct, but the pipeline applies the operator in the wrong direction. A rate of 1.25 can mean 1 EUR equals 1.25 USD, or it can mean 1 USD equals 1.25 of another currency. The difference is not semantic decoration; it decides whether the transformation multiplies or divides. This guide gives data engineers an explicit modeling rule, a small hypothetical retail example, and diagnostics that catch multiplication-versus-division errors before they become trusted reporting facts.

sections.heading: The rule is about units, not currency-pair labels
paragraphs: The safest way to model an exchange rate is to store the units that the number represents. A currency pair label such as EURUSD is not enough because different feeds and teams can interpret it differently. One team may read EURUSD as USD per EUR. Another may read it as EUR per USD. Both can be internally consistent, but a shared warehouse cannot depend on that convention being remembered correctly in every query.

Use numerator and denominator currency columns instead of an overloaded pair string. Define the stored rate as rate_value numerator_currency per 1 denominator_currency. That gives the rate a physical unit, such as USD per EUR or CAD per USD. Once the unit is explicit, the operator follows from the position of the transaction currency: if the transaction amount is in the denominator currency and the target is the numerator currency, multiply; if the transaction amount is in the numerator currency and the target is the denominator currency, divide.

This article is limited to arithmetic direction and numeric modeling. It does not decide whether a transaction should use a transaction-date rate, a reporting-date rate, an average rate, a tax rate, or an accounting policy. Those are separate business and finance decisions. The data engineering contribution here is to make the chosen rate unambiguous and mechanically hard to misuse.
bullets: Store rate_value with an explicit unit: numerator_currency per 1 denominator_currency.
Multiply when converting from denominator_currency to numerator_currency.
Divide when converting from numerator_currency to denominator_currency.
Treat inversion as 1 divided by the rate, not as a sign change, pair-name swap, or formatting operation.
Do not aggregate mixed-currency local amounts before conversion.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail orders table that must normalize local order totals to USD. The rate table stores a decimal rate_value with the unit numerator_currency per denominator_currency. The example deliberately includes both directions: EUR and JPY are stored as USD per local currency, while CAD is stored as CAD per USD. That means EUR and JPY orders convert to USD by multiplication, but the CAD order converts by division.

The intended calculations are straightforward when written with units. For order 101, 80 EUR times 1.25 USD per EUR equals 100 USD. For order 102, 135 CAD divided by 1.35 CAD per USD equals 100 USD. For order 103, 10,000 JPY times 0.0067 USD per JPY equals 67 USD. The correct normalized total is 267 USD before any USD-native orders are added.

The counterexamples show why a single operator rule such as always multiply or always divide is dangerous. If the CAD row is always multiplied, 135 CAD becomes 182.25 USD instead of 100 USD. If the JPY row is always divided, 10,000 JPY becomes 1,492,537.31 USD instead of 67 USD. That is not a rounding problem; it is a unit problem.

The following SQL is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, aligned with PostgreSQL 18 numeric documentation for exact decimal arithmetic. It is not evidence of execution. It is written as a compact fixture that a team could adapt into a unit test or model assertion.

codeExamples.code:
with orders as (
  select * from (values
    (101, 'EUR',  80.00::numeric),
    (102, 'CAD', 135.00::numeric),
    (103, 'JPY', 10000.00::numeric)
  ) as t(order_id, local_currency, amount_local)
), rates as (
  select * from (values
    ('USD', 'EUR', 1.25000000::numeric),  -- 1 EUR = 1.25 USD
    ('CAD', 'USD', 1.35000000::numeric),  -- 1 USD = 1.35 CAD
    ('USD', 'JPY', 0.00670000::numeric)   -- 1 JPY = 0.0067 USD
  ) as t(numerator_currency, denominator_currency, rate_value)
), normalized as (
  select
    o.order_id,
    o.local_currency,
    o.amount_local,
    r.numerator_currency,
    r.denominator_currency,
    r.rate_value,
    case
      when o.local_currency = r.denominator_currency
       and r.numerator_currency = 'USD'
        then o.amount_local * r.rate_value
      when o.local_currency = r.numerator_currency
       and r.denominator_currency = 'USD'
        then o.amount_local / r.rate_value
      else null
    end as amount_usd_correct,
    o.amount_local * r.rate_value as amount_if_always_multiply,
    o.amount_local / r.rate_value as amount_if_always_divide
  from orders o
  join rates r
    on o.local_currency in (r.numerator_currency, r.denominator_currency)
   and 'USD' in (r.numerator_currency, r.denominator_currency)
)
select
  order_id,
  local_currency,
  round(amount_usd_correct, 2) as amount_usd_correct,
  round(amount_if_always_multiply, 2) as amount_if_always_multiply,
  round(amount_if_always_divide, 2) as amount_if_always_divide
from normalized
order by order_id;

sections.heading: A schema pattern that prevents operator guessing
paragraphs: A resilient schema separates the local monetary fact from the normalized reporting fact. This is consistent with dimensional modeling guidance for multiple currencies: keep the true local-currency fact and also provide a standardized converted fact for cross-currency reporting. The local value preserves what happened in the source system. The normalized value supports aggregation in a common currency.

For the rate table, avoid a single column named pair and a second column named rate. Those names push the most important meaning into tribal knowledge. Prefer columns that force the unit into the data model: numerator_currency, denominator_currency, rate_value, effective date or interval, source, and any approved rate type. If the target currency is USD, a row with numerator_currency = USD and denominator_currency = EUR means multiply EUR amounts by rate_value. A row with numerator_currency = CAD and denominator_currency = USD means divide CAD amounts by rate_value.

Store monetary amounts and rates in exact decimal types where your warehouse supports them. PostgreSQL’s numeric type is documented as an exact numeric type suitable when exactness is required, with configurable precision and scale. That does not remove the need for business rounding rules, but it avoids introducing binary floating-point artifacts into currency normalization. A common practical pattern is to calculate in higher precision than display precision, then round at defined output boundaries. For example, do not round every intermediate converted line to two decimals unless that is the agreed business rule.

The rate table should also make inversion explicit. If you need the inverse of 1.25 USD per EUR, compute 1 / 1.25 = 0.8 EUR per USD and store or derive it with its own numerator and denominator. Never assume that swapping a pair label is sufficient. The numeric value must change, and repeated inversion plus premature rounding can create avoidable differences.
bullets: Recommended monetary fact columns: amount_local, local_currency, amount_reporting, reporting_currency, rate_id.
Recommended rate columns: numerator_currency, denominator_currency, rate_value, rate_type, valid_from, valid_to, source_system.
Recommended constraint: numerator_currency and denominator_currency must differ except for an explicit identity-rate convention.
Recommended calculation: derive amount_reporting from one joined rate row, not from a pair-name parsing rule in every dashboard.

sections.heading: Diagnostics for wrong direction
paragraphs: A wrong-direction conversion is often deterministic, so ordinary freshness and null checks will not find it. The rows are present. The rates are populated. The dashboard may even reconcile for currencies whose stored direction happens to match the developer’s assumption. The check must target the arithmetic contract.

Start with a small control fixture like the hypothetical one above. Include at least one row that should multiply and at least one row that should divide. The expected values should be hand-calculated and stored as test data or model assertions. A fixture with only EUR to USD at USD per EUR will not catch an always-multiply implementation because always-multiply is correct for that one shape.

Add a round-trip diagnostic, but understand its limits. If the model converts 80 EUR to 100 USD using 1.25 USD per EUR, then 100 divided by 1.25 returns 80 EUR. If the model converts 135 CAD to 100 USD using 1.35 CAD per USD, then 100 multiplied by 1.35 returns 135 CAD. This check can catch inconsistent operator use between forward and reverse logic. It does not prove that the original rate row was the right business rate or the right date; it only verifies that the unit contract is internally consistent.

Magnitude checks are useful as a second layer. A 10,000 JPY retail order converted to 1,492,537.31 USD is suspicious even without knowing today’s actual exchange rate. These checks should use domain-specific bands, not universal currency assumptions. For example, a luxury wholesale order and a small online retail order have different plausible ranges. When a row violates the band, write an error event or quarantine record with the order id, currency, rate id, operator branch, and computed amount. Kimball’s error event schema guidance is useful background for modeling such data-quality events as analyzable facts rather than discarded log lines.
bullets: Control fixture: include both multiply and divide cases with expected normalized amounts.
Round-trip check: convert back to the local amount using the inverse operator and compare within the approved rounding tolerance.
Magnitude check: flag normalized values outside plausible business ranges for the dataset.
Coverage check: ensure every non-reporting currency row joins exactly one approved rate row for the chosen conversion rule.
Lineage check: persist rate_id with the converted fact so a suspicious amount can be traced to the exact unit and value used.

codeExamples.code:
with converted as (
  select * from (values
    (101, 'EUR', 80.00::numeric, 'USD', 'EUR', 1.25000000::numeric, 100.00::numeric),
    (102, 'CAD', 135.00::numeric, 'CAD', 'USD', 1.35000000::numeric, 100.00::numeric),
    (103, 'JPY', 10000.00::numeric, 'USD', 'JPY', 0.00670000::numeric, 67.00::numeric)
  ) as t(order_id, local_currency, amount_local, numerator_currency, denominator_currency, rate_value, amount_usd)
)
select
  order_id,
  case
    when local_currency = denominator_currency
      then round(amount_usd / rate_value, 2)
    when local_currency = numerator_currency
      then round(amount_usd * rate_value, 2)
  end as amount_local_reconstructed,
  round(amount_local, 2) as amount_local_expected,
  case
    when case
      when local_currency = denominator_currency
        then round(amount_usd / rate_value, 2)
      when local_currency = numerator_currency
        then round(amount_usd * rate_value, 2)
    end = round(amount_local, 2)
    then 'pass'
    else 'fail'
  end as round_trip_check
from converted
order by order_id;

sections.heading: Aggregation and rounding tradeoffs
paragraphs: The operator rule must be applied at the same grain as the rate decision. If orders in the same report use different currencies or different rate rows, convert each row or each agreed fact grain first, then aggregate the normalized amount. Summing 80 EUR, 135 CAD, and 10,000 JPY into 10,215 local units and then trying to convert the total is meaningless because the sum has no single currency unit.

There is a real tradeoff between reproducibility and precision. Storing both local and normalized facts makes reports faster and easier to reconcile, but it means the normalized number is a persisted result of a specific rate, operator branch, and rounding rule. Recomputing on the fly reduces stored facts but increases the chance that different consumers choose different joins, rates, or operators. For governed reporting, persisting the normalized amount with rate_id and calculation metadata is often easier to audit.

Rounding should be treated as a separate rule from direction. Direction tells you whether to multiply or divide. Numeric representation controls whether the calculation can represent the needed decimal precision. Rounding decides how many decimals are retained for storage, reporting, settlement, or display. Mixing these concerns hides bugs: a wrong-direction JPY conversion cannot be fixed by changing scale from two decimals to six decimals.

The practical design target is simple: someone reading one row in the rate table should be able to say the rate out loud with units, choose the operator mechanically, and reconstruct the normalized fact later. If that is not possible, the model is still relying on convention rather than data.

takeaways: Exchange-rate direction is a unit-modeling problem: store rates as numerator currency per denominator currency so multiplication and division are mechanically determined.
Use hypothetical control rows that include both multiply and divide cases; a test set with only one direction can let an always-multiply or always-divide bug pass.
Persist local amount, local currency, normalized amount, reporting currency, and rate_id so converted facts can be audited and reconstructed.
Use exact decimal numeric types and defined rounding boundaries; precision choices do not compensate for applying the rate in the wrong direction.

title: Geometric means for compounded growth
description: A practical guide to spotting when arithmetic averages misstate compounded change, with counterexamples, calculation rules, and an illustrative SQL pattern for growth metrics.
lead: Arithmetic averages are often harmless for additive quantities. They become dangerous when a metric changes by repeated multiplication. If a dashboard says the average monthly growth rate is 10%, that does not mean the metric compounded as if it grew 10% every month. For compounded growth, practitioners need the product of period factors, or the geometric mean of those factors, not the arithmetic mean of the percent changes.

sections.heading: The symptom: an average growth rate that cannot reproduce the ending value
paragraphs: A useful test for any reported average growth rate is simple: if you apply it repeatedly from the starting value, does it reproduce the ending value? If not, the average is probably answering a different question than the one readers think it answers.

Consider a hypothetical retail metric: active subscriptions at the end of each month. Suppose the business starts with 100 active subscriptions. Month 1 grows by 50%, month 2 shrinks by 40%, and month 3 grows by 20%. The arithmetic average of the three monthly growth rates is 10%: (50% - 40% + 20%) / 3 = 10%.

But the compounded path is not 100 growing by 10% three times. The actual path is 100 × 1.50 × 0.60 × 1.20 = 108. The ending value is 108, an 8% cumulative increase. If someone applies the arithmetic average as a representative monthly growth rate, they get 100 × 1.10 × 1.10 × 1.10 = 133.10. That is not a rounding issue; it is the wrong aggregation rule.

The geometric mean fixes the question. Convert each growth rate to a growth factor, multiply the factors, then take the nth root. For the example, the compounded factor is 1.08. The equivalent constant monthly factor is 1.08^(1/3), approximately 1.025986. The equivalent constant monthly growth rate is therefore about 2.60%, not 10%. Applied three times, that rate reproduces the observed ending value: 100 × 1.025986^3 = 108, allowing for normal decimal rounding.

sections.heading: The calculation rule: average factors geometrically, not percent changes arithmetically
paragraphs: Use the geometric mean when each period changes the base for the next period. That is the defining feature of compounding. Revenue growth, customer-base growth, retention decay, index returns, inventory shrinkage, and conversion-rate lift over sequential stages can all involve multiplicative factors, depending on the modeled process.

Let r_i be the growth rate for period i. The corresponding factor is g_i = 1 + r_i. A 25% increase is a factor of 1.25. A 25% decrease is a factor of 0.75. The cumulative factor over n periods is g_1 × g_2 × ... × g_n. The equivalent constant per-period factor is (g_1 × g_2 × ... × g_n)^(1/n). The equivalent constant per-period growth rate is that value minus 1.

This is the geometric mean of the positive factors, not the geometric mean of the raw percentage values. NIST describes the geometric mean as the nth root of the product of n observations, commonly applied to positive values. That positivity requirement matters in data engineering work because ordinary real-valued logarithms and geometric means do not accept zero or negative factors.

The shortest counterexample is a 50% gain followed by a 50% loss. The arithmetic average return is 0%: (50% - 50%) / 2 = 0%. But a value of 100 becomes 150 after the gain, then 75 after the loss. The cumulative factor is 1.50 × 0.50 = 0.75. The equivalent constant per-period factor is sqrt(0.75), about 0.8660, so the equivalent per-period growth rate is about -13.40%. A flat 0% average return would imply the value ended at 100, which is false.

This is also why the order of growth rates does not affect the final compounded product when the same factors are applied to the whole base, but the arithmetic average still fails to represent the compounding effect. A 50% loss followed by a 50% gain also ends at 75. Multiplication of the factors is commutative; averaging the rates is simply not the correct operation for cumulative change.
bullets: Convert rates to factors before aggregation: r becomes 1 + r.
Multiply factors to compute cumulative change.
Use the nth root of the product to compute the equivalent constant period factor.
Subtract 1 only at the end to return from factor space to rate space.
Do not use a geometric mean when any factor is zero or negative without an explicit business rule for that case.

sections.heading: When arithmetic averages are still the right tool
paragraphs: The practical rule is not “geometric means are better.” The rule is “match the aggregation to the question.” Arithmetic averages remain appropriate for additive measurements and for some questions about expected one-period observations.

If the metric is order value, delivery time, number of items per basket, or support tickets per account, the arithmetic mean may be the natural summary because the values are not being repeatedly applied to a changing base. For example, three hypothetical orders of $20, $30, and $40 have an average order value of $30. There is no compounding process in that calculation.

Arithmetic averages can also be meaningful when the question is cross-sectional rather than cumulative. If a table contains one monthly growth rate per store and the analyst asks, “What was the unweighted average store growth rate this month?”, the arithmetic mean answers that narrow question. It does not answer, “How much did the whole portfolio grow?” unless all stores have equal starting bases or a separate weighting rule makes that true.

Here is a hypothetical retail counterexample. Store A grows from 100 to 200 orders, a 100% increase. Store B falls from 900 to 810 orders, a 10% decrease. The unweighted arithmetic average of store growth rates is 45%. But the combined business grows from 1,000 to 1,010 orders, which is only 1%. The 45% figure describes the average of two store-level rates; it does not describe total order growth. For total growth, aggregate the numerator and denominator first, then compute the rate.

This distinction is one of the most common modeling failures in metric layers. A rate is often a ratio with a denominator. Averaging ratios without checking the denominators can produce a number that is mathematically valid but operationally misleading. For cumulative time-series growth, the denominator problem is joined by compounding: each period’s ending value becomes the next period’s starting value.

sections.heading: A diagnostic checklist for growth metrics
paragraphs: Before publishing an average growth rate, ask what the number will be used to infer. If readers will use it to explain how a starting value became an ending value, the arithmetic average is suspect. If readers will compare a typical one-period observation, it may be acceptable, but the label should make that clear.

A reliable diagnostic is to reconstruct the end state. Start with the initial value, apply the reported average for the reported number of periods, and compare the result with the actual ending value. A large difference means the label “average growth” is probably ambiguous or wrong. This check is small enough to add to metric review, dbt model tests, dashboard QA, or semantic-layer validation.

The next diagnostic is to inspect the domain of the factors. A growth rate of -100% creates a factor of zero. A rate below -100% creates a negative factor, which is usually invalid for ordinary compounded growth of counts, balances, or positive-valued measures. These rows require a business decision, not a quiet formula. Common choices include treating the series as terminated, excluding the segment from a compounded-rate summary, reporting cumulative change directly, or redesigning the metric.

The final diagnostic is grain. If growth is calculated per customer, store, product, or campaign, decide whether the metric is meant to summarize a typical entity or the total population. A typical-entity summary may average entity-level rates. A population growth metric should usually aggregate the starting and ending quantities at the population grain, then compute the rate. Time compounding and cross-sectional weighting are separate issues, but they often appear in the same dashboard.
bullets: Will the reported average be used to reproduce an ending value from a starting value? If yes, use compounded factors.
Are all growth factors positive? If no, do not blindly apply a geometric mean.
Are the periods equally spaced? If no, consider a duration-aware annualized or per-day convention.
Are rates being averaged across entities with different denominators? If yes, decide whether the desired metric is entity-typical or population-total.
Does the dashboard label distinguish arithmetic average growth from equivalent compounded growth? If no, clarify it.

sections.heading: Illustrative SQL pattern for compounded growth
paragraphs: In SQL, compounded growth is often easier to express with logarithms than with a direct product aggregate. The identity is that the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms. So instead of multiplying every factor directly, compute EXP(SUM(LN(factor))). This pattern also makes the aggregation shape clear: first convert rates to factors, then aggregate in factor space, then convert back to rates.

The following is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, aligned with PostgreSQL 18 aggregate function naming such as SUM, AVG, and COUNT. It is not presented as execution evidence. The hypothetical input contains one row per period with a decimal growth rate, such as 0.50 for 50% and -0.40 for -40%. The WHERE clause enforces the ordinary positive-factor requirement for a real-valued geometric mean. In a production model, rejected rows should be surfaced rather than silently ignored.

codeExamples.code:
WITH monthly_growth AS (
    SELECT 1 AS month_index, 0.50::numeric AS growth_rate
    UNION ALL SELECT 2, -0.40::numeric
    UNION ALL SELECT 3, 0.20::numeric
), valid_factors AS (
    SELECT
        month_index,
        growth_rate,
        1.0 + growth_rate AS growth_factor
    FROM monthly_growth
    WHERE 1.0 + growth_rate > 0
), compounded AS (
    SELECT
        COUNT(*) AS periods,
        AVG(growth_rate) AS arithmetic_avg_growth,
        EXP(SUM(LN(growth_factor))) AS cumulative_factor
    FROM valid_factors
)
SELECT
    periods,
    arithmetic_avg_growth,
    cumulative_factor,
    POWER(cumulative_factor, 1.0 / periods) - 1.0 AS equivalent_periodic_growth
FROM compounded;

sections.heading: Model the question, not just the formula
paragraphs: A growth metric should make its interpretation hard to misuse. “Average monthly growth” is ambiguous. “Arithmetic average of monthly growth rates” is precise but often not what executives, analysts, or downstream models need. “Equivalent compounded monthly growth rate” is longer, but it tells the reader the number is designed to reproduce cumulative change over the interval.

For data models, store enough information to recompute the metric at the right grain. Keeping only a pre-averaged growth rate removes the denominators and period factors needed to correct mistakes later. Prefer storing starting value, ending value, period start, period end, and entity grain. Derived rates can then be calculated consistently for dashboards and downstream tables.

Also separate cumulative change from equivalent periodic change. Cumulative change answers, “How much did the value change over the whole interval?” Equivalent periodic change answers, “What constant per-period rate would produce that same change?” Those are related but not interchangeable. In the earlier hypothetical example, cumulative change is 8%, while equivalent monthly growth is about 2.60%. Reporting one as the other changes the meaning.

Finally, avoid using the geometric mean as a cosmetic replacement for uncomfortable arithmetic. If a product line goes to zero, a customer cohort disappears, or a return factor becomes non-positive, the data is telling you about a boundary condition. The correct response is an explicit rule and a clear label, not a formula that hides the event.

takeaways: Arithmetic averages misstate compounded growth when period rates are repeatedly applied to a changing base.
For compounded growth, convert rates to positive factors, multiply the factors, take the nth root for an equivalent constant period factor, and subtract 1 at the end.
Always distinguish cumulative change, equivalent compounded periodic growth, and an arithmetic average of period or entity rates.
When rates are averaged across entities with different denominators, aggregate the underlying counts or values first if the goal is population-level growth.
Zero or negative growth factors are modeling boundary cases; they require an explicit business rule rather than a blind geometric mean.

title: Missing measurements versus measured zero
description: A practical guide to modeling unavailable observations separately from true zero activity, with numeric counterexamples and explicit aggregation rules.
lead: A zero says the system observed no activity. A missing measurement says the system does not know what happened. Treating both as the same value can make totals look complete, averages drift downward, and inactivity rates look worse than they are. The repair is not complicated: model observation state separately from the numeric measure, and make every aggregate state its denominator and coverage rule.

sections.heading: The failure mode: zero is a value, not a fallback
paragraphs: In analytical data, null and zero answer different questions. Zero is a measured numeric value: the store had no sales, the sensor counted no events, or the customer made no purchases during an observed interval. Missing means the measurement is unavailable: the feed failed, the event window has not closed, the upstream source omitted the row, or the value was suppressed by a quality rule.

The difference becomes dangerous when a data pipeline uses COALESCE(amount, 0) early and stores the result as if it were the original fact. That transformation is sometimes convenient for charts, but it destroys information. Afterward, a real zero and an unknown value are indistinguishable unless a separate status column preserved the distinction.

This article is limited to numeric representation and aggregation. It is not tax advice, accounting policy, or a general metric-definition guide. The practical goal is narrower: keep unavailable observations distinct from real absence of activity so that downstream calculations can say what they know, what they do not know, and how much coverage supports the answer.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical daily sales table for two stores over five days. Each store-day is expected to have one observation. A measured zero means the store-day was observed and no sales occurred. An unavailable value means the store-day should have been observed but the measurement is missing.

For Store A, the five expected daily sales amounts are 100, 0, unavailable, 40, and 60. For Store B, they are unavailable, 0, 0, 50, and 50. The observed sales total is 200 for Store A and 100 for Store B, for a combined observed total of 300. But that 300 is not the same as a complete five-day total, because two of the ten expected observations are unavailable.

Now compare the averages. Store A has four measured days, so its observed average is 200 divided by 4, which is 50. If the unavailable day is silently converted to zero, the average becomes 200 divided by 5, which is 40. Store B has an observed average of 100 divided by 4, which is 25. If its unavailable day is treated as zero, the average becomes 20. Combined, the observed average is 300 divided by 8, or 37.5. The coerced average is 300 divided by 10, or 30.

The zero-day rate is distorted too. Store A has one measured zero among four measured days, so its measured zero-day rate is 25 percent. Store B has two measured zero days among four measured days, so its measured zero-day rate is 50 percent. Combined, the measured zero-day rate is 3 divided by 8, or 37.5 percent. If missing values are treated as zeros, the combined rate becomes 5 divided by 10, or 50 percent. The metric now says activity was absent more often than the data actually observed.

The important point is not that nulls always change sums. In this example, the observed sum and the null-as-zero sum are both 300. The problem is that the coerced sum is easy to mislabel as complete. For additive measures, replacing missing with zero may leave the arithmetic total unchanged while still erasing the coverage warning that the total is partial.

sections.heading: Model the observation state separately from the measure
paragraphs: A reliable design separates the value from the observation state. The numeric measure answers, “what value was observed?” The status answers, “was the observation available?” These columns should enforce a simple invariant: measured observations have a numeric value, and unavailable observations do not pretend to have one.

For many pipelines, two states are enough: measured and unavailable. Some domains need more states, such as not_applicable, pending, suppressed, or invalid. Add those only when they change calculation rules. For example, a store that was not yet open may be not_applicable rather than unavailable. A source file that failed to arrive is unavailable. A store open for business with no transactions is measured with value zero.

Avoid encoding these states by overloading the number itself. Do not use -1, 999999, or 0 as a sentinel for missingness in a measure column. Sentinel values leak into aggregates, require every consumer to remember special cases, and often fail when a legitimate value later overlaps the sentinel. Null is a better representation for “no measured numeric value,” but null alone is usually not enough. Pair it with an explicit status or reason so that missingness can be counted, explained, and tested.
bullets: Use a nullable numeric measure for the observed value.
Use a non-null observation_status column for measured, unavailable, or other approved states.
Add a check constraint or equivalent data quality rule tying status to value presence.
Carry expected observation grain explicitly, such as one row per store per day when that grain is required.
Publish coverage fields next to metrics whose inputs can be unavailable.

sections.heading: Calculation rules that preserve meaning
paragraphs: Once the data model keeps value and state separate, aggregation rules become explicit. The rule should name the numerator, denominator, and treatment of unavailable observations. If a metric cannot be safely interpreted without full coverage, return a partial result with coverage, or return no final result until coverage passes the required threshold.

For an additive observed measure, compute observed_sum as the sum of measured values only. Also compute expected_count, measured_count, unavailable_count, and coverage_ratio. Do not call observed_sum a complete total unless measured_count equals expected_count or a documented estimation method fills the gap. A partial total can still be useful, but it should not masquerade as a complete total.

For an average over observations, divide by measured_count, not expected_count. If the business question is “average sales on measured store-days,” unavailable days are outside the denominator. If the business question is “average sales per expected store-day,” then unavailable observations prevent a complete answer unless an explicit imputation or estimation rule is part of the metric definition.

For a zero-activity rate, count measured zeros in the numerator and measured observations in the denominator. Unavailable observations belong in a separate coverage calculation. This prevents a monitoring gap from being reported as customer inactivity, store inactivity, or product inactivity.

For coverage, use expected_count as the denominator. Coverage is measured_count divided by expected_count. This is the metric that should fall when observations are unavailable. Do not hide that fall by pushing missing values into the zero bucket.

There is one more edge case worth making explicit: no input rows. PostgreSQL documents that aggregate functions such as sum return null rather than zero when there are no rows, while count returns zero. That behavior is useful because an empty input is not automatically a measured zero. If a presentation layer wants to display 0 for a missing aggregate, that should be a final formatting choice with a label, not a fact-table rewrite.

sections.heading: Illustrative PostgreSQL implementation
paragraphs: The following illustrative SQL uses PostgreSQL 18 documentation semantics for numeric types and aggregate functions. It is a compact example, not an execution transcript. The dataset is hypothetical.

The table stores one expected store-day per row. The check constraint preserves the invariant: measured rows must have a value, and unavailable rows must not store a numeric value. The queries then calculate observed values and coverage side by side.

For the hypothetical data, the expected result by store is: Store A has expected_count 5, measured_count 4, unavailable_count 1, observed_sales 200.00, observed_average_sales 50.00, measured_zero_day_rate 0.25, coverage_ratio 0.80, and null_as_zero_average 40.00. Store B has expected_count 5, measured_count 4, unavailable_count 1, observed_sales 100.00, observed_average_sales 25.00, measured_zero_day_rate 0.50, coverage_ratio 0.80, and null_as_zero_average 20.00. Across both stores, expected_count is 10, measured_count is 8, unavailable_count is 2, observed_sales is 300.00, observed_average_sales is 37.50, measured_zero_day_rate is 0.375, coverage_ratio is 0.80, and null_as_zero_average is 30.00.

codeExamples.code:
create table fact_store_day_sales_hypothetical (
    store_id text not null,
    sales_date date not null,
    observation_status text not null check (observation_status in ('measured', 'unavailable')),
    sales_amount numeric(12, 2),
    unavailable_reason text,
    primary key (store_id, sales_date),
    check (
        (observation_status = 'measured' and sales_amount is not null)
        or
        (observation_status = 'unavailable' and sales_amount is null)
    )
);

insert into fact_store_day_sales_hypothetical
    (store_id, sales_date, observation_status, sales_amount, unavailable_reason)
values
    ('A', date '2026-01-01', 'measured',    100.00, null),
    ('A', date '2026-01-02', 'measured',      0.00, null),
    ('A', date '2026-01-03', 'unavailable',   null, 'source_file_missing'),
    ('A', date '2026-01-04', 'measured',     40.00, null),
    ('A', date '2026-01-05', 'measured',     60.00, null),
    ('B', date '2026-01-01', 'unavailable',   null, 'pos_feed_late'),
    ('B', date '2026-01-02', 'measured',      0.00, null),
    ('B', date '2026-01-03', 'measured',      0.00, null),
    ('B', date '2026-01-04', 'measured',     50.00, null),
    ('B', date '2026-01-05', 'measured',     50.00, null);

select
    store_id,
    count(*) as expected_count,
    count(*) filter (where observation_status = 'measured') as measured_count,
    count(*) filter (where observation_status = 'unavailable') as unavailable_count,
    sum(sales_amount) filter (where observation_status = 'measured') as observed_sales,
    avg(sales_amount) filter (where observation_status = 'measured') as observed_average_sales,
    (
        count(*) filter (where observation_status = 'measured' and sales_amount = 0)
    )::numeric
        / nullif(count(*) filter (where observation_status = 'measured'), 0)
        as measured_zero_day_rate,
    (
        count(*) filter (where observation_status = 'measured')
    )::numeric
        / nullif(count(*), 0)
        as coverage_ratio,
    avg(coalesce(sales_amount, 0)) as null_as_zero_average
from fact_store_day_sales_hypothetical
group by store_id
order by store_id;

sections.heading: A diagnostic for existing pipelines
paragraphs: To find this problem in an existing warehouse, look for places where null-handling happens before the semantic layer or metric query. Early null replacement is not always wrong, but it should be suspicious when it happens in staging tables, fact tables, or reusable marts without a companion availability flag.

The diagnostic question is simple: after this transformation, can a downstream query still tell the difference between “we observed zero” and “we did not observe”? If not, the pipeline has collapsed two states into one. The fix may require backfilling only a status column, not reworking every metric at once.

Start with metrics where the denominator matters: averages, rates, percentages, service levels, and inactivity measures. Totals are not immune, but denominator-based metrics usually expose the distortion faster. Then add coverage reporting to dashboards and data products that depend on incomplete feeds. A partial metric with visible coverage is usually more honest than a clean-looking number built from silent zeros.
bullets: Search transformations for COALESCE(measure, 0), IFNULL(measure, 0), NVL(measure, 0), and default-zero schema rules.
Check whether fact tables have explicit expected grain rows or only rows for observed activity.
Compare count(*) with count(measure) for nullable measures; a gap often indicates unavailable observations.
Calculate zero_count and null_count separately before any dashboard formatting.
Require metric definitions to state whether unavailable observations are excluded, estimated, blocked, or reported through coverage.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: Keeping missingness explicit adds columns, constraints, and aggregation fields. It also forces product and analytics teams to face incomplete data instead of hiding it. That is a feature, not a drawback, when the alternative is publishing false inactivity.

The main tradeoff is usability. Many users want one number. Data engineers can still provide one number when the metric definition supports it, but the number should carry its coverage or eligibility rule. For example, a dashboard can show observed sales and coverage together, or it can suppress the final metric until coverage reaches a documented threshold. What it should not do is silently turn missing measurements into zero activity.

Dimensional models often represent facts at a declared grain, such as store-day or transaction-line. When observations arrive late or are corrected, the model needs a way to preserve the grain while marking the current measurement state. That design is compatible with incremental and real-time fact loading patterns, but the important principle is independent of tooling: the row’s existence, the value’s numeric amount, and the observation’s availability are separate ideas.

takeaways: A measured zero means activity was observed and the value was zero; a missing measurement means the value is unknown or unavailable.
Do not use zero as a default for unavailable numeric facts in reusable tables. Preserve an explicit observation status and calculate coverage.
For averages and zero-activity rates, use measured observations as the denominator and report unavailable observations separately.
For totals, distinguish an observed partial sum from a complete total. Equal arithmetic does not imply equal meaning.
Use constraints, tests, or semantic-layer rules to prevent measured and unavailable states from being collapsed before aggregation.

title: Event time versus processing time
description: A practical guide to modeling two clocks in data systems: when an event happened and when your platform observed it, using a hypothetical retail fixture with late arrivals, retries, and replayed history.
lead: Most timestamp bugs start with a quiet substitution: a pipeline uses the time a row arrived as if it were the time the customer action happened. That may be harmless for some operational checks, but it is wrong for many facts, metrics, and backfills. The practical fix is not a more elaborate schedule. It is a data model that preserves both clocks and makes their meaning visible.

sections.heading: The two clocks answer different questions
paragraphs: Event time is when the action represented by a record occurred. If a customer placed an order at 23:59:50, that is the order’s event time, even if the event did not reach the warehouse until several minutes later. Processing time is when a system observed, ingested, transformed, or loaded the record. A single business event can have several processing timestamps as it moves through collectors, queues, staging tables, and modeled tables.

The distinction matters because the two clocks support different decisions. Event time answers business questions such as how many orders happened on Tuesday, which promotion was active when a click occurred, or whether a shipment was late relative to the order. Processing time answers operational questions such as when the pipeline first saw the record, whether an upstream system is delayed, or which records were included in a particular load.

A robust model does not choose one clock and discard the other. It names them according to their role. Prefer specific columns such as order_placed_at, event_occurred_at, source_observed_at, ingested_at, loaded_at, and transformed_at over a generic timestamp column. Generic names hide semantics and make it easy for later queries to group by the wrong time.

This article deliberately stays at the time-semantics level. It does not cover UTC storage boundaries, daylight-saving edge cases, or orchestration scheduling. Those are adjacent problems, but they are not substitutes for separating when an action happened from when systems noticed it.

sections.heading: A hypothetical fixture with late arrival, retry, and replay
paragraphs: Consider this hypothetical retail event stream. The fixture uses UTC timestamps to avoid mixing this topic with local reporting boundaries. The important point is not the time zone; it is that event_occurred_at and observed_at are intentionally different fields.

Rows: 1) source_event_id=e-100, event_type=order_placed, order_id=o-100, event_occurred_at=2026-03-31T23:58:40Z, observed_at=2026-03-31T23:58:43Z, load_id=L1. 2) source_event_id=e-101, event_type=order_placed, order_id=o-101, event_occurred_at=2026-04-01T00:01:05Z, observed_at=2026-04-01T00:01:10Z, load_id=L1. 3) source_event_id=e-102, event_type=order_placed, order_id=o-102, event_occurred_at=2026-03-31T23:59:50Z, observed_at=2026-04-01T00:04:20Z, load_id=L2. 4) source_event_id=e-100, event_type=order_placed, order_id=o-100, event_occurred_at=2026-03-31T23:58:40Z, observed_at=2026-04-01T00:06:00Z, load_id=L2. 5) source_event_id=e-099, event_type=order_placed, order_id=o-099, event_occurred_at=2026-03-30T21:15:00Z, observed_at=2026-04-01T00:10:00Z, load_id=L2. 6) source_event_id=e-103, event_type=order_cancelled, order_id=o-103, event_occurred_at=2026-04-01T00:02:30Z, observed_at=2026-04-01T00:02:31Z, load_id=L1.

The rows are intentionally troublesome. Row 3 happened on March 31 but arrived on April 1. Row 4 is a retry of row 1 with the same source event identifier. Row 5 is older history replayed into the system on April 1. Row 6 is a different event type, included to show why filtering by business event type still matters.

If the business question is, how many orders were placed on March 31, the event-time answer is two: o-100 and o-102. If a query uses observed_at instead, the answer is one, because o-102 was not observed until April 1. Neither answer is universally correct. They answer different questions. The event-time count describes customer activity. The observed-time count describes what the platform had seen by the end of March 31.

Now ask an operational question: how many order_placed events did the platform observe on April 1? Before deduplication, it observed four order_placed records: e-101, e-102, the retry of e-100, and e-099. After deduplicating by source_event_id, it observed three distinct order_placed events for the first time on April 1: e-101, e-102, and e-099. That observed-time diagnostic is useful for pipeline operations, but it should not be confused with an April 1 sales metric.

sections.heading: Query the same records two ways
paragraphs: The following PostgreSQL-style example is illustrative. It uses a small common table expression to make the fixture self-contained and a window function to keep the first observation of each source_event_id. PostgreSQL documents date and time types separately from window functions; the important modeling point here is the partitioning of meaning, not a claim about query tuning.

First, deduplicate retries using processing metadata, then group business activity by event time. The expected order_placed counts are: 2026-03-30 has 1, 2026-03-31 has 2, and 2026-04-01 has 1. The March 31 count includes e-102 even though the system observed it on April 1.

codeExamples.code:
WITH hypothetical_events(source_event_id, event_type, order_id, event_occurred_at, observed_at, load_id) AS (
  VALUES
    ('e-100', 'order_placed',    'o-100', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-31 23:58:40+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-31 23:58:43+00', 'L1'),
    ('e-101', 'order_placed',    'o-101', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:01:05+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:01:10+00', 'L1'),
    ('e-102', 'order_placed',    'o-102', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-31 23:59:50+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:04:20+00', 'L2'),
    ('e-100', 'order_placed',    'o-100', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-31 23:58:40+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:06:00+00', 'L2'),
    ('e-099', 'order_placed',    'o-099', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-30 21:15:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:10:00+00', 'L2'),
    ('e-103', 'order_cancelled', 'o-103', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:02:30+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:02:31+00', 'L1')
), first_observation AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (
    SELECT
      hypothetical_events.*,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY source_event_id
        ORDER BY observed_at ASC, load_id ASC
      ) AS observation_rank
    FROM hypothetical_events
  ) ranked
  WHERE observation_rank = 1
)
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('day', event_occurred_at) AS event_day,
  COUNT(*) AS placed_orders
FROM first_observation
WHERE event_type = 'order_placed'
GROUP BY event_day
ORDER BY event_day;

sections.heading: The counterexample: grouping by arrival and calling it history
paragraphs: A common failure mode is to partition, aggregate, or overwrite historical facts by processing time while labeling the output as event history. In the fixture, a daily sales model grouped by observed_at would report one order on March 31 and three distinct first-observed orders on April 1 after deduplication. That may look plausible, but it is not a count of orders placed on those days.

The bug becomes more damaging during replays and backfills. Row 5 occurred on March 30 but was observed on April 1. If a replayed historical event is grouped by observed_at, old business activity appears as new business activity. Dashboards can show a false spike, downstream features can learn the wrong recency, and reconciliation against source-of-truth reports becomes confusing because everyone is using the word day to mean something different.

Processing time is still valuable. It should be used to answer questions such as which batch introduced the record, how long the source-to-staging delay was, and what the system knew at a particular cutoff. For example, latency can be measured as observed_at minus event_occurred_at when both timestamps are trustworthy. In the fixture, e-102 has a delay of 4 minutes and 30 seconds: it occurred at 23:59:50 and was observed at 00:04:20. That delay is an operational signal, not a reason to move the order into April’s event-time sales.

A useful diagnostic is to produce both views side by side for a small fixture before modeling the full table. If event_day and observed_day totals are identical for every test case, the fixture is probably too easy. Include at least one late event, one retry, and one replayed historical event. The goal is not to make the query complicated; it is to force the model to reveal which clock each calculation uses.

codeExamples.code:
WITH first_observation AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (
    SELECT
      hypothetical_events.*,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY source_event_id
        ORDER BY observed_at ASC, load_id ASC
      ) AS observation_rank
    FROM hypothetical_events
  ) ranked
  WHERE observation_rank = 1
)
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('day', observed_at) AS observed_day,
  COUNT(*) AS distinct_orders_first_observed
FROM first_observation
WHERE event_type = 'order_placed'
GROUP BY observed_day
ORDER BY observed_day;

-- Expected result for the fixture after deduplication:
-- 2026-03-31 00:00:00+00 => 1
-- 2026-04-01 00:00:00+00 => 3

sections.heading: Modeling rules that prevent clock mixing
paragraphs: The first rule is to make timestamp names specific enough that a reviewer can tell what they mean without reading pipeline code. If the column means the customer action time, name it after the action, such as order_placed_at, or use a clearly documented event_occurred_at. If the column means the collector received the message, use observed_at or source_observed_at. If the column means the warehouse inserted the row, use loaded_at. Avoid using created_at unless the creating actor is unambiguous.

The second rule is to preserve the original event timestamp even when records arrive late. Do not overwrite event_occurred_at with the load time to make partitions convenient. If the source did not provide a trustworthy event timestamp, represent that uncertainty explicitly with a null, a quality flag, or a separate inferred timestamp. Quietly substituting processing time creates facts that look precise but are semantically wrong.

The third rule is to choose deduplication order intentionally. In the fixture, retaining the earliest observed_at for each source_event_id answers when the platform first saw the event. A different use case might retain the latest observation if later records can correct earlier payloads. That is a business and source-system decision, not a property of event time itself.

The fourth rule is to keep metric grouping and operational monitoring separate. Business metrics such as orders placed, signups completed, and payments authorized usually group by event time. Pipeline health metrics such as records ingested, load duration, and source delay usually group by processing time. A single table can support both, but a single timestamp column cannot faithfully represent both.

Stream processing frameworks also make this distinction explicit. Spark Structured Streaming, for example, documents event-time windows and watermarking concepts around event timestamps. That vocabulary is useful even outside Spark: late data handling should be described relative to event time, while system observation and load cutoffs should be described relative to processing time.
bullets: Name timestamps by role: occurred, observed, ingested, loaded, transformed.
Use event time for business history unless the question is explicitly about system observation.
Use processing time for operational diagnostics, freshness checks, load auditing, and reproducible cutoffs.
Do not fill a missing event time with processing time without labeling it as inferred or unknown.
Test models with late arrivals, retries, and replayed history before trusting daily aggregates.

sections.heading: A short review checklist
paragraphs: Before approving a model that contains time-based facts, ask five questions. What real-world action does the event timestamp represent? Which system assigned the processing timestamp? Can one business event appear more than once with different observed_at values? What should happen when a record arrives after the event-time reporting window has closed? Are backfilled records allowed to change historical event-time metrics?

Those questions keep the conversation focused. The issue is not whether March 31 or April 1 is the right day in the abstract. The issue is which clock the question is asking for. In the fixture, March 31 is the right event day for e-102, and April 1 is the right observed day. Both are true. A correct model lets downstream users choose deliberately instead of inheriting an accidental timestamp from the ingestion path.

takeaways: Event time records when the business action happened; processing time records when a system observed, loaded, or transformed the record.
Late arrivals, retries, and replays are the easiest way to expose timestamp confusion in a model review.
Business history usually groups by event time, while pipeline diagnostics and reproducible cutoffs usually use processing time.
Never replace a missing or inconvenient event timestamp with a processing timestamp without making that inference explicit.
